assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned superconducting circuits into a controllable platform for light-matter interaction: strong coupling between an artificial atom and a single microwave photon, dispersive readout and the transmon-era architecture. It opened a genuinely new regime (strong, tunable coupling in a solid-state circuit) and underpins both microwave quantum optics and most current superconducting quantum processors. Its scientific core is the discovery of that regime, not merely the application to quantum computing.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf's 2004 proposal and the Wallraff et al. 2004 strong-coupling experiment are the decisive pair. Of the supplied names, Schoelkopf (experimental development and the transmon with Yale colleagues), Wallraff (first strong-coupling experiment) and Blais (theory) form a coherent trio. Allocation relative to other contributors (e.g. Girvin, Devoret) is delicate and not fully resolved in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended across dozens of laboratories for over twenty years; the interpretation is completely stable. Timeliness is a concern: the 2025 prize already rewarded superconducting-circuit quantum physics, so the committee must judge whether this is distinct enough and not premature repetition.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and my own closeness to this community, which I should declare and weigh carefully.
Girvin and Devoret are not among the supplied names, so the credit set may be incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened an entirely new, tunable platform for strongly correlated physics: flat bands predicted by theory, then correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity observed in 2018. It spawned the large field of moire quantum materials and is a clear case of a prediction followed by dramatic experimental discovery.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald's 2011 continuum-model prediction of flat bands at magic angles, and Cao, Jarillo-Herrero et al. 2018 for the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity. MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero capture theory plus experiment. Eva Andrei's early STM evidence of flat-band localization is a legitimate competing claim; Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers is not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced by many groups and quickly extended to related moire systems. The nature of the superconducting pairing is still debated, but the discovery of the phenomena is robust. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the prize goes to the flat-band prediction, the experimental discovery, or both; Andrei's claim is unresolved.
The microscopic mechanism of the superconductivity remains open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide clean, tunable quantum simulators of Hubbard-type models, exemplified by the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This gave physics a new way to study many-body quantum matter and has been a lasting and general contribution.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization; Greiner, Bloch et al. 2002 observed the Mott transition; Bloch led the broader programme and Greiner pioneered the microscope. Esslinger (fermions) and Cirac are also credited, so a three-person selection necessarily leaves out important contributors. Zoller's and Cirac's roles overlap with the trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, confirmed by many independent groups, and now a standard tool. Recognition is arguably somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Choosing three from five credited people is contentious.
Overlap in the Cirac and Zoller credit across several quantum-simulation candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators identified a new class of quantum matter characterized by topology rather than symmetry breaking, with protected edge or surface states. It is a conceptually deep, clearly Nobel-worthy discovery with a clean theory-to-experiment narrative.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele's 2005 theoretical papers, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal (not in the supplied credit), and Konig et al. 2007 from Molenkamp's group form the quantum spin Hall core. Hasan's 3D topological insulator work is a competing credit. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are the cleanest theory-plus-first-experiment trio but omit Zhang (deceased), Hasan and Moore/Balents.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed in HgTe and in 3D materials by ARPES and transport. Mature, with a fully stable interpretation. Recognition is timely, if not somewhat late.
uncertainties: Allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and others not in the list is disputed.
The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions may be viewed by some members as partly overlapping.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks with the magic-wavelength concept brought fractional frequency uncertainty to the 1e-18 level, enabling tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. The idea is original and the impact on precision measurement is large and measurable.
assessment.attribution: Katori's 2003 proposal of the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye's realization and record-precision development with strontium are clearly decisive. The two-person configuration is natural, though Hall and Hansch (frequency combs, 2005) are already honoured and others such as Ludlow and Kimble also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across multiple laboratories and compared at the 1e-18 level; the redefinition of the second is still pending, but the physics is established and robust.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as an instrument or metrology advance rather than a discovery.
Competition from ion clocks (Wineland-related work was recognized in 2012).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics established radiation-pressure cooling of mechanical oscillators to the quantum ground state and quantum control of macroscopic mechanical motion, linking optics, mechanics and superconducting circuits. This is close to my own experience with phonons coupled to artificial atoms, and it is a rich physical regime.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg, Vahala and Aspelmeyer demonstrated radiation-pressure back-action and sideband cooling; Painter's group contributed ground-state cooling and nanoscale optomechanical crystals. The three names are a plausible set, but important roles (Vahala, Schwab, Cleland, Lehnert, Teufel) are not in the credit and the allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by several groups, with ground-state cooling, squeezing and entanglement all reproduced. Technological applications (gravitational-wave detectors, transduction) are maturing, but the field is still developing.
uncertainties: Multiple strong contributors outside the supplied credit, making a clean trio difficult.
Whether it is a single discovery or a collection of advances.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays provide a route to controlled quantum many-body simulation and quantum computation with hundreds of atoms. The scientific novelty (blockade-based gates and strongly interacting programmable arrays) is substantial and growing, though much of the visible impact is recent.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller et al. 2000 proposed Rydberg gates; Saffman, Walker and Browaeys demonstrated blockade; Lukin's group demonstrated large programmable arrays and quantum phases. Credit among Lukin, Zoller, Browaeys, Saffman is intertwined; Bernien, Endres and others at Harvard and Caltech are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Replicated in multiple groups and rapidly evolving. Interpretations are stable, but fault-tolerant demonstrations are ahead of us, so I consider it slightly premature compared to the others.
uncertainties: Large amounts of recent work still in flux; the decisive step is not yet settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantized conductance of ballistic quantum point contacts in steps of 2e^2/h was a clean, striking demonstration of Landauer-type transport in mesoscopic conductors, and it is the entry point into modern mesoscopic physics, including the 0.7 anomaly and the quantum devices used in spin and Majorana experiments. As someone who started in mesoscopic transport theory, I find it foundational.
assessment.attribution: The two nearly simultaneous 1988 papers, van Wees et al. (Delft) and Wharam et al. (Cambridge), established it; Pepper led the Cambridge group. Theoretical developments by Landauer and Buttiker and the earlier work are essential context but not credited. Van Wees, Wharam and Pepper capture the experimental discovery.
assessment.maturity: Extremely mature and reproduced in all high-mobility 2DEG systems. The discovery is old, so timing is a concern, and it has been regarded more as a foundational tool than as a new regime.
uncertainties: Long delay since 1988 and whether the committee considers it still a priority.
Wharam's and others' contributions relative to Landauer-Buttiker theory are not fully resolved.
